skill.name: Main idea vs interesting detail
skill.why: Finding the main idea helps you remember what a whole text is about.
skill.how: Find the big point most sentences back up. A fact that doesn't is a fun extra.

steps.say: Here's my wombat fact file. First, what is every sentence about?

show.text: Their bums are as hard as rock.
Their poo comes out in cubes.

steps.ask: Pick what the text is about.

options.text: wombats
rocks
options.reason: Rock only comes up once. What is every sentence about?

options.text: poo
options.reason: Poo only comes up once. What is every sentence about?

steps.win: Yes! Wombats. What a text is about, in a word or two, is the topic.

steps.say: But what does the text SAY about wombats? I look for the big point.

show.nudge: Thick skulls is one example. Which sentence do the examples back up?

show.text: Their bums are as hard as rock.
show.nudge: A rock-hard bum is one example. Which sentence does it back up?

show.text: Their poo comes out in cubes.
show.nudge: Cube poo is fun, but it isn't the big point. Try again.

steps.ask: Tap the sentence the others back up.
steps.win: Yes! That's the main idea: the big point a text makes about its topic.

steps.say: Careful! Gus says the main idea is just 'wombats'. Is he right?
steps.ask: Which one is the main idea?

options.text: wombats
options.reason: That's the topic. It only names what the text is about. What does it say?

options.text: Wombats are built tough.
Wombat poo comes out in cubes.
options.reason: That's one fun fact. Do the other sentences back it up?

steps.win: Yes! A topic is a word or two. A main idea is a whole point about the topic.

steps.say: Funny doesn't mean extra. Ask: does it show wombats are tough?

show.nudge: That's the main idea itself. Find a detail that backs it up.

show.text: Their bums are as hard as rock.
Their poo comes out in cubes.
show.nudge: Cube poo is funny, but does it show wombats are tough?

steps.ask: Tap the funny detail that backs up the main idea.
steps.win: Yes! A rock-hard bum is funny, AND it shows they're tough. So it backs it up.

steps.say: Last wombat sentence. It is true, and very fun. Where does it go?

show.text: Their poo comes out in cubes.

steps.ask: Which box does the cube poo go in?

options.text: main idea
options.reason: Do the other sentences back up cube poo? Find the big point.

options.text: detail that backs it up
options.reason: Does cube poo show wombats are tough? Ask the question.

options.text: fun extra

steps.win: Yes! It doesn't show they're tough. A true fact that doesn't back up the main idea is a fun extra.

steps.say: Your turn. Here's my footy report. Find the big point.

show.text: The Rays run ten kilometres at training.
show.nudge: Ten kilometres is one example. What big point does it back up?

show.text: They are the fittest team around.
They never run out of breath.
show.nudge: That's one example. Which sentence does it back up?
A goose doesn't make the team fit. That's a fun extra.

steps.win: Yes! Running and never running out of breath both back it up. The goose is a fun extra. Honk!

terms.means: What the text is about, in a word or two.
The big point the text makes about its topic. Most sentences back it up.
A detail that shows the main idea is true. It can be funny!
A true, fun fact that doesn't back up the main idea.

examples.text: Their bums are as hard as rock.
Their poo comes out in cubes.
They are the fittest team around.
They run ten kilometres at training.

card.test: Find the sentence most others back up. That's the main idea. Funny can still back it up.

weDo.text: Sharks are amazing hunters. They can smell blood from far away. They can feel tiny movements in the water. One shark was found with a number plate in its tummy.
weDo.hint: Which one do most of the sentences back up?
weDo.success: Smelling and feeling both show sharks are great hunters. The number plate is just a fun extra.

options.text: Sharks are amazing hunters.
A shark swallowed a number plate.
options.reason: That's a fun fact about one shark. It isn't about hunting at all.

options.text: Sharks can smell blood.
options.reason: That's one way sharks hunt. The main idea covers all of them.

weDo.text: Mo's kitchen is a disaster. The sink is full of green water. A sock is stuck to the ceiling. Mo's goldfish is called Captain Crunch.
weDo.prompt: Put each sentence in the right box.
weDo.hint: Does it show the kitchen is a disaster, or is it just fun?
weDo.success: 'A disaster' sums it up. The sink and the sock show the mess. The goldfish is a fun extra.

items.text: Mo's kitchen is a disaster.
items.reason: This is the big point about the kitchen. The mess details back it up.

items.text: The sink is full of green water.
items.reason: Green water in the sink is part of the mess. It shows the disaster.

items.text: A sock is stuck to the ceiling.
items.reason: Funny, but it's still part of the mess, so it backs up the main idea.

items.text: Mo's goldfish is called Captain Crunch.
items.reason: A fun fact, but a goldfish's name doesn't show the kitchen is a mess.

creature.name: Gistling
creature.blurb: A wedge-tailed eagle chick that flies high enough to see the whole paddock, not just one shiny beetle. It hunts for the big idea.

write.ask: Write the main idea these three details back up. Make it one whole sentence.
given: Cockatoos can flip open wheelie bins with their beaks.
They learn the trick by watching other cockatoos.
Some even work out how to push bricks off the lids.
checks: My sentence is a whole point, not just a topic
All three details back it up
It doesn't just repeat one detail
write.model: Cockatoos are clever at working out how to break into bins.

encounters.frame: Wren pins a fact card on the wall of the island animal clinic.
encounters.text: Koalas are champion sleepers. They can snooze for up to twenty hours a day. Their leafy food gives them very little energy, so resting saves it. They wedge their bums into a fork in the tree so they don't fall out. Then they wake up, munch some leaves and nod off again. A koala at our clinic once slept through a thunderstorm. Even loud trucks don't wake them.
encounters.prompt: What is the main idea?
encounters.success: Nearly every sentence is about koalas sleeping: how long, why, where and how deeply.

options.text: Koalas sleep for most of the day.
One koala at the clinic slept through a thunderstorm.
options.reason: That's a fun story about one koala. The card is about all koalas.

options.text: Koalas wedge themselves into tree forks.
options.reason: That's how they stay safe while they sleep. It's one detail, not the whole card.

encounters.frame: Mo is reading his cooking diary out loud. The Gistling looks worried.
encounters.prompt: Tap the sentence that tells the main idea.
encounters.success: Most sentences show one pancake going wrong. 'A total failure' sums them all up.

parts.tap: My pancakes today were a total failure.
I flipped the first one so hard it stuck to the ceiling.
parts.reason: This is one pancake. Find the sentence that covers all of them.

parts: It is still up there now.

parts.tap: The second one came out black on both sides.
parts.reason: That's only the second pancake. The main idea covers every pancake.

parts.tap: The dog sniffed the third one and walked away.
parts.reason: A funny detail about the third pancake, not the whole diary.

parts: Gus wants to keep it for a slime experiment.

parts.tap: At least my cup of tea was nice.
parts.reason: The tea is an extra at the end. The diary is about the pancakes.

encounters.frame: Zed is writing a report for the space station noticeboard. It needs a heading.
encounters.text: Living in space is really strange. You can't pour a drink, because the water floats away in blobs. You sleep in a bag strapped to the wall. Your face gets puffy and your legs get skinny. Even going to the toilet needs a special fan to suck everything away. One astronaut said the worst part was missing the smell of rain.
encounters.prompt: Which heading fits best?
encounters.success: Drinks, sleep, faces and toilets are all strange bits of daily life in space.

options.text: Everyday life is weird in space
The space toilet fan
options.reason: The toilet gets only one sentence. A heading should cover the whole report.

options.text: Why one astronaut misses the smell of rain
options.reason: That's how one astronaut felt. What are most of the sentences about?

encounters.frame: Gus's poster for the slime lab has fallen apart. Help the Gistling sort the bits.
encounters.text: Snot is actually useful. It traps dust and germs before they get into your lungs. It also stops the inside of your nose from drying out. You make about a cup of it every day. Gus once sneezed so hard that his snot hit the whiteboard. Some snails make slime that is a bit like snot. When you're sick, your snot can turn green. That green colour comes from the germ fighters in it.
encounters.prompt: Put each sentence in the right box.
encounters.success: One sentence sums up the poster. Two show how snot helps. Two are just fun extras.

items.text: Snot does a useful job in your body.
items.reason: The poster opens with this, then shows how snot protects you.

items.text: Snot traps dust and germs before they reach your lungs.
items.reason: Trapping germs is one useful job, so it backs up the main idea.

items.text: Gus once sneezed snot onto the whiteboard.
items.reason: Funny, but it doesn't show how snot helps your body.

items.text: Snot stops your nose from drying out.
items.reason: Keeping your nose from drying out is another useful job.

items.text: Some snails make slime like snot.
items.reason: Snails are a side fact. The poster is about how your snot helps you.

encounters.frame: Tully is reading the Reef Rays match report on the island radio.
encounters.text: The Reef Rays won the final with the last kick of the game. They were two points behind with ten seconds left. Jai took a mark right in front of goal. The crowd went silent. He kicked it straight through the middle. The siren went, and the whole team piled on top of him. Someone's dog ran onto the ground and joined in.
encounters.prompt: What is the main idea?
encounters.success: Every sentence builds up to, or follows, the winning kick in the final seconds.

options.text: The Reef Rays won with the last kick.
A dog ran onto the ground.
options.reason: That's a funny extra at the end. What do most sentences build up to?

options.text: Jai took a mark right in front of goal.
options.reason: That's one step on the way. The report is about how the final was won.

encounters.frame: Wren found an old note pinned to the lighthouse door.
encounters.prompt: Tap the sentence that tells the main idea.
encounters.success: Creaky stairs, a flickering light, cold wind and a torch turning off are all strange things after dark.

parts.tap: The old lighthouse was painted red and white in 1902.
parts.reason: This is about the paint, not about what the note is warning you.

parts.tap: These days, strange things happen inside it after dark.
The stairs creak when nobody is on them.
parts.reason: That's one strange thing. Look for the sentence they all fit under.

parts: A light flickers at the top, but there are no bulbs. Cold wind blows inside, even with the windows shut.

parts.tap: Last week, my torch turned itself off three times.
parts.reason: That happened on one night. It's a detail that backs up the main idea.

parts.tap: I'm never going back, not even for my lost thong.
parts.reason: This is how the writer feels at the end, not what the note is about.

encounters.frame: The Gistling found a soggy flyer stuck to the jetty.
encounters.text: Lots of people think the ocean floor is dark and empty. In fact, the deep sea is packed with strange life. Anglerfish dangle glowing lures in front of their mouths. Giant tube worms grow taller than a person beside hot vents. Some jellyfish flash blue lights like a disco when something bumps them. There are even squid with eyes as big as dinner plates. Scientists think most deep-sea animals haven't been found yet. One scientist named a new fish 'Lumpy Dave' because nobody could think of anything nicer. Every dive brings up something new, and some of it is very, very ugly.
encounters.prompt: What is the main idea?
encounters.success: Anglerfish, worms, jellyfish and squid all back up one point: the deep sea is crowded with weird life.

options.text: The deep sea is full of strange creatures.
Some deep-sea squid have eyes as big as dinner plates.
options.reason: That's one creature. Count the others the flyer lists. What do they all show?

options.text: People think the ocean floor is empty.
options.reason: The flyer starts with this idea only to show that it's wrong.

encounters.frame: Zed posted a game review on the island noticeboard.

encounters.success: Changing tunnels, hats, the boss and playing with a friend all back up Zed's big opinion.

parts.tap: I've played Mole Mayhem for three weeks straight.

parts.tap: My little brother just calls it 'the dirt game'.
parts.reason: A funny extra about his brother, not the point of the review.

parts.tap: Honestly, it's the best digging game I have ever played.
The tunnels change every time, so no two levels are the same.
parts.reason: This is one reason the game is good. Look for the sentence they all back up.

parts.tap: The moles have silly hats you can unlock, like a tiny pirate hat.
parts.reason: The hats are a fun detail that supports Zed's opinion.

parts.tap: The boss worm at the end is huge and really, really hard to beat.
parts.reason: This describes one part of the game, not the whole review.

parts.tap: Best of all, you can dig with a friend on the same screen.
parts.reason: This is his favourite reason, but it's still one reason, not his overall opinion.

parts.tap: It did crash once, but only when my dog sat on the screen.
parts.reason: A funny moment, not what the review is mostly saying.

parts.tap: Next week I'm reviewing a game about angry pigeons.

encounters.frame: Maxx Vantablack is live-streaming from his secret lab. Sounds dodgy.
encounters.text: Hey, Vantafam! Today I'm showing you my brand-new robot helper, Clank. I built it myself in only two weeks, with a bit of help from my mum. Clank can carry fifty kilos without breaking a sweat. Not that robots sweat. It can sneak through jungles silently on its rubber feet. It even has night-vision eyes that glow green. It has a net launcher in each arm and a cage in its belly. Clank is perfect for catching rare creatures, and I mean rescuing them. Totally rescuing. It also makes a pretty decent toastie. Smash that like button, and you might see Clank in action this week.
encounters.prompt: What is the main idea of Maxx's stream?
encounters.success: Nets, a cage, silent feet and glowing eyes all point to one job: catching creatures.

options.text: Maxx's new robot is built to catch creatures.
Maxx's robot makes a decent toastie.
options.reason: A funny extra. Look at the nets and the cage. What are they for?

options.text: Maxx wants more people to smash the like button.
options.reason: He asks for likes at the end, but the stream is about what Clank does.

encounters.frame: Indi made a poster for the island band night. The Gistling wants it sorted.
encounters.text: Our school band is ready for the big concert on Friday night. We have practised every lunchtime for six weeks. Everyone now knows all four songs by heart. We even ran a full dress rehearsal on Tuesday, and nothing went wrong. Our drummer has fixed the snare drum that Gus accidentally filled with slime. The new speakers have arrived, and they are seriously loud. Mr Pappas has even ironed his lucky purple shirt. Last year a seagull landed on the trumpet player mid-song, but we have a net now. Doors open at six, and tickets are two dollars at the office.
encounters.prompt: Put each sentence in the right box.
encounters.success: Practice, a perfect rehearsal and new speakers show the band is ready. The seagull is a fun extra.

items.text: The band is ready for Friday's concert.
items.reason: Most of the poster shows how the band got ready, so this sums it up.

items.text: The band has practised every lunchtime for six weeks.
items.reason: All that practice is one reason the band is ready.

items.text: A seagull once landed on the trumpet player.
items.reason: That's a funny story from last year. It doesn't show the band is ready.

items.text: The dress rehearsal went without a single mistake.
items.reason: A perfect rehearsal shows the band is ready for the real thing.

items.text: The new speakers have arrived.
items.reason: The gear is ready too, so this backs up the main idea.

encounters.frame: Wren is writing a Field Guide page about ibis. She needs a heading.
encounters.text: White ibis used to live mostly in wetlands far from towns. When droughts dried those wetlands out, many flew to the cities. Now they are everywhere. They tip over bins with their long curved beaks. They have learned to wake up early on bin day. They steal chips straight out of people's hands at the beach. They nest in park trees and raise their chicks next to busy roads. Their feathers often look grubby, but they don't seem to mind. Some people call them 'bin chickens', which is a bit rude. One ibis in our town even learned to open a lunchbox. City life suits them perfectly.
encounters.prompt: Which heading fits best?
encounters.success: The page moves from wetlands to cities and shows all the ways ibis now live there.

options.text: How ibis took over the city
The ibis that opened a lunchbox
options.reason: That's what one ibis did. A heading should cover the whole page.

options.text: Why ibis are called bin chickens
options.reason: The nickname gets one sentence. Where do most of the sentences say ibis live now?

parts.reason: This describes one part of the mural. It backs up the main idea.

parts.tap: Its eyes seem to follow you down the street.

parts.tap: Up close, you can even see tiny fish hiding between the scales.
parts.reason: Another single detail. Look for the sentence they all support.

encounters.frame: Gus is reading a news report out loud while eating his lunch. Bad timing.
encounters.text: In the 1960s, Australian farmers had a smelly problem. Millions of cow pats were drying out in paddocks and lasting for months. Our native dung beetles were used to small, dry kangaroo droppings, not big, wet cow pats. Some paddocks were so crusted with old pats that cows refused to graze there. The pats smothered the grass and became nurseries for swarms of bush flies. So scientists brought in dung beetles from Africa and Europe. More than forty kinds were released across the country. It worked brilliantly. Today, these hardworking beetles can bury a fresh cow pat in as little as a day. They roll it into balls, drag it underground and lay their eggs inside. This puts goodness back into the soil, helps grass grow and leaves the flies with nowhere to breed. Some dung beetles can pull more than a thousand times their own body weight. Next time you see one, say thanks.
encounters.prompt: What is the main idea?
encounters.success: The report sets up a poo problem, then shows how the beetles fixed it. That's the big idea.

options.text: Imported dung beetles fixed Australia's cow-pat problem.
Australia's paddocks were once covered in cow pats.
options.reason: That's the problem at the start. The report goes on to show how it was solved.

options.text: Some dung beetles can pull a thousand times their weight.
options.reason: An amazing fact, but it's one detail about strength, not the point of the report.

options.text: Native dung beetles prefer kangaroo droppings.
options.reason: This explains why the problem started. It's a detail inside the story.

encounters.frame: Zed found a page of the space station's logbook floating near the airlock.

parts.tap: Mission control on Earth suggested turning the station off and on again.
parts.reason: A funny bit of bad advice. It's a detail.

parts.tap: Engineer Petrov spent two hours crawling through a tunnel no wider than a pizza box.
parts.reason: This is one person's part in the search, not the main idea.

parts.tap: At the far end, she pulled out half a ham sandwich with mustard still on it.

parts: Petrov said it smelled like a sock that had been to the gym.

parts.tap: The kitchen camera showed it drifting away while everyone was watching the footy.
parts.reason: This explains how the sandwich got loose. It's a supporting detail.

parts: Nobody has owned up to losing it. The filter is now clear, and the air is fresh again.

parts.tap: Petrov has asked for a medal and a fresh sandwich, without mustard.
parts.reason: A funny detail about Petrov. Which sentence sums up the whole morning?

parts.tap: In the end, one floating sandwich caused the whole morning's emergency.

encounters.frame: Tully is writing a team profile for the Reef Rays club newsletter.
encounters.text: Most footy teams hate the rain, but the Reef Rays seem to love it. When the ground turns to mud, other teams drop marks and miss easy kicks. The Reef Rays just keep going. Last season they played six games in the wet and won every one of them. Their nickname around the league is now 'the Ducks'. Their coach says it's no accident. On rainy Tuesday nights, while other clubs cancel training, the Rays are out on the oval practising slippery handballs in the dark. They even train with a ball that's been soaked in a bucket of soapy water. Their ruckman, Big Benny, once slid ten metres on his bum and still got the ball away. On dry days, the team is only average, winning about half its games. But when the clouds roll in, opposition fans start to worry. Rain is forecast for Saturday's final, and the whole island is excited.
encounters.prompt: What is the main idea?
encounters.success: Wet wins, soapy-ball training and worried fans all show the Rays are at their best in rain.

options.text: The Reef Rays play best in wet weather.
Rain makes footy harder for most teams.
options.reason: True, but the profile says this to show how different the Reef Rays are.

options.text: The Reef Rays train in the rain on purpose.
options.reason: This explains why they're good in the wet. It's a supporting detail.

options.text: The Reef Rays and the rain
options.reason: That's the topic, in a few words. What big point does the profile make about it?

encounters.frame: Mo's restaurant review is pinned up in the galley. The Gistling wants it sorted.
encounters.text: I've eaten fish and chips all over the island, and I'm the ship's cook, so trust me. The Salty Gull on the jetty serves the best fish and chips I have ever tasted. Last week I ate there three times. The batter is so crunchy you can hear it from the next table. The fish comes fresh off the boats each morning, still smelling of the sea. Even the chips are perfect: fat, golden and salty, with crispy little bits at the bottom of the bag. The potato cakes are also really excellent, if you can keep them away from the birds. The owner, Stavros, has a parrot that shouts 'Vinegar!' at every customer. Tables fill up fast, so get there before noon. Watch out for the seagulls, because they are bold, hungry and organised. One stole a potato cake right out of my mouth. I would still go back tomorrow.
encounters.prompt: Put each sentence in the right box.
encounters.success: Batter, fresh fish and three visits in a week back up the claim. The birds are fun extras.

items.text: The Salty Gull serves the best fish and chips Mo has ever tasted.
items.reason: Most of the review backs this up, so it's the main idea.

items.text: A parrot shouts 'Vinegar!' at every customer.
items.reason: A funny extra about the shop. It doesn't show the food is the best.

items.text: The batter is so crunchy you can hear it.
items.reason: Crunchy batter is one reason the food is so good.

items.text: A seagull stole a potato cake out of Mo's mouth.
items.reason: A funny moment, but it says nothing about how good the food is.

items.text: The fish comes fresh off the boats each morning.
items.reason: Fresh fish is another reason the fish and chips are the best.

items.text: Mo ate there three times last week.
items.reason: Would Mo go back three times in one week if the food weren't great?

encounters.frame: Wren is making a Field Guide page about a creepy cave. It needs a heading.
encounters.text: Walk into Hollowgum Cave at night and switch off your torch. At first there is total darkness. Then, slowly, thousands of tiny blue lights appear on the roof, like a sky full of stars. It looks magical, but it is actually a deadly trap. Each light belongs to a glow-worm, which isn't really a worm at all but the larva of a small fly. The glow-worm hangs dozens of sticky threads, like fishing lines, from the cave roof. Flying insects head for the light, thinking it is the night sky, and get stuck. The glow-worm then reels the line in and eats its catch alive. Hungry glow-worms glow brighter. Visitors are asked to whisper, because loud noises can make the lights dim. Bats sleep near the entrance, so watch your head on the way in. Some people say the cave is haunted, but the only thing hunting in there is the glow-worms.
encounters.prompt: Which heading fits best?
encounters.success: Most of the page explains how the lights lure and catch insects. That's the big idea.

options.text: The cave lights that trap their dinner
Is Hollowgum Cave haunted?
options.reason: Ghosts get one line at the end, and the page says the cave isn't haunted.

options.text: Why the cave lights scare insects away
options.reason: The page says the lights draw insects in so they get stuck, not scare them away.

options.text: Watch out for bats at the entrance
options.reason: Bats get one line near the end. What do most sentences say the lights do?

encounters.frame: Gus is reading a news report about the island's new robot lifeguard.

parts.tap: It also found a lost toddler in minutes by scanning the crowd for a red hat.
parts.reason: One great rescue. Which sentence do all the rescues back up?

parts.tap: Its cameras spotted a rip that the human lifeguards had missed, and it moved the flags in seconds.

parts.tap: Its cameras can see through thick sea spray from two hundred metres away.

parts.reason: A funny problem, and the only one. Find the sentence all the good news backs up.

parts: Kids lined up for photos with it all afternoon, and one man said it gave better advice than his doctor. The council says Splash runs on solar panels and can work for twelve hours without a break.

encounters.frame: The Gistling swoops down on a page torn from a wildlife magazine.
encounters.text: Stand quietly in a wet forest in winter and you might hear a kookaburra, a whipbird, a camera shutter and a car alarm. All of them are coming from the same bush. The performer is a male superb lyrebird, and he is not showing off for you. Every sound in his act is aimed at one audience: the females nearby. In winter, each male scratches out a small stage of bare dirt, then sings, dances and fans his spectacular tail over his head. A young male's act is patchy, with a few borrowed calls and plenty of mistakes. Older males have spent years collecting sounds, and their copies are so accurate that other birds sometimes fly in to answer them. Mimicry, in other words, is his way of proving he's the most experienced male around. Females wander from stage to stage, listening closely, and they choose the males whose shows are longest and most convincing. One researcher recorded a male who copied twenty different species in a single performance. Some lyrebirds are said to mimic chainsaws, though scientists still argue about how often that really happens. People love lyrebirds for their tricks, but for the bird himself the whole concert has a single purpose: winning a mate.
encounters.prompt: What is the main idea?
encounters.success: The article keeps returning to the females and ends by naming his single purpose: winning a mate.

options.text: A male lyrebird's copied sounds are a performance to win a mate.
People love lyrebirds for all the clever tricks and sounds they can copy.
options.reason: The last sentence says people love the tricks. But what does it say the tricks are for?

options.text: Older lyrebirds make better copies than young ones.
options.reason: This is one supporting detail about how skill grows. It doesn't cover the whole article.

options.text: Scientists disagree about whether lyrebirds copy chainsaws.
options.reason: That's a side note near the end, not what the article is mostly about.

encounters.prompt: Indi says the main idea is Tully's last sentence, about car parks. Zed says it's the sentence asking for a music studio. Why is Zed right?
encounters.success: A main idea can be a request. Every reason in the letter backs up Tully's ask for a studio.

options.text: The studio sentence comes near the start, which is where a letter's main idea goes.
options.reason: A main idea can come anywhere. Position isn't the test. Which sentence do the others back up?

options.text: The car park sentence is a fun extra, like the possums that enjoy music.
options.reason: The possums are the fun extra. The car park line is a real reason for the studio.

options.text: Nearly every other sentence, even the car park one, is a reason for the studio.
The studio sentence names the topic, and the topic is the main idea.
options.reason: The topic is the boatshed, in a word or two. The main idea is the point Tully makes.

encounters.text:
Dear Councillors,

Last month, the council announced that the old boatshed would be knocked down to make room for twelve more car parks. I am writing to ask you to turn it into a music studio for young people instead. Right now, the nearest place to practise the drums is a forty-minute ferry ride away. My cousin rehearses in his garage, and his neighbours have complained to the police four times. Last year, three of our students made the state finals for music, and they all had to practise in cupboards. The boatshed already has power, a solid floor and thick walls that would keep the noise from bothering anyone. The roof leaks a little, but my uncle is a builder and says he can fix it cheaply. Local musicians have offered to run free lessons on weekends, and the school band has promised to help paint it. A studio would give teenagers somewhere to go on Friday nights besides the servo car park. There is also a family of possums living in the rafters, and they seem to enjoy music. Twelve car parks would be full for an hour on market day, but a studio would be full every single night.

Tully

encounters.frame: Zed is reading a magazine article out loud on the deck, to nobody in particular.
encounters.text: Watch a speedrunner finish a game that takes most players twenty hours in under fifteen minutes, and you'd swear they must have lightning-fast fingers. Their reflexes are quick, but that isn't really the secret. The secret is research. Top runners study a game like scientists study a new beetle, poking every wall, ledge and door to see what happens. They replay the same ten seconds thousands of times and record the results in enormous spreadsheets. It is slow, careful and, honestly, a bit boring to watch. That patient testing is how they discover glitches, such as a spot where you can clip through a wall and skip an entire level. Once someone finds a new trick, the whole community shares it, studies it and tries to improve it. Then the record tumbles again. Some games have been tested so thoroughly that runners know exactly how many frames each jump takes. The current record holder for Turbo Toad Kingdom, a fourteen-year-old from Ballarat, says she spent more time reading forum posts than actually playing. She also says her cat has never once let her finish a practice run in peace. So the next time you see a jaw-dropping record, remember that it was built through months of testing, not one lucky moment.
encounters.prompt: What is the main idea?
encounters.success: The article says the secret is research, then shows testing, spreadsheets and studying. That's the main idea.

options.reason: The article says this is what people assume, then says it isn't the real secret.

options.text: Speedrunners use glitches to skip whole levels.
options.reason: Glitches are one thing testing uncovers. They're a detail, not the main point.

options.reason: Sharing is one part of the story. What does the article call the real secret?

encounters.frame: The Gistling found a report from the reef station. Sort the big idea, the backing and the extras.
encounters.text: Most people walk straight past sea cucumbers. They look like soggy sausages lying on the sand, and they hardly move. They come in many colours, from plain brown to bright orange with blue spots. But without these lumpy creatures, coral reefs would be in serious trouble. A sea cucumber spends its day swallowing sand and digesting the tiny scraps of dead plants and animals in it. Then it poos out clean sand behind it. A single sea cucumber can clean dozens of kilograms of sand every year. Its droppings also release nutrients that help nearby coral and seagrass grow. Without them, waste would pile up on the sea floor, and the coral would struggle to grow. Sea cucumbers have some revolting habits, too. Many breathe through their bottoms. Some shoot out their own sticky guts to tangle attackers, then grow new ones. A small fish called a pearlfish sometimes lives inside a sea cucumber's bottom and pops out at night to feed. In some places, so many sea cucumbers have been collected that the sand around reefs has turned smelly and murky. Those murky reefs prove the point: a reef with no sea cucumbers is like a city where nobody takes out the rubbish.
encounters.prompt: Put each sentence in the right box.
encounters.success: Clean sand and feeding coral back up the big idea, poo and all. Other gross habits are fun extras.

items.text: Sea cucumbers do a cleaning job that keeps coral reefs healthy.
items.reason: The report builds to this and ends by comparing reefs without them to a city full of rubbish.

items.text: Many sea cucumbers breathe through their bottoms.
items.reason: A revolting habit, but it has nothing to do with why reefs need them.

items.text: A sea cucumber poos out clean sand behind it.
items.reason: Gross, yes. But does pooing out clean sand help keep the reef healthy?

items.text: A pearlfish sometimes lives inside a sea cucumber.
items.reason: A gross, surprising fact, but it doesn't show how they help the reef.

items.text: Their droppings release nutrients that help coral and seagrass grow.
items.reason: Feeding the coral is another way they keep the reef healthy.

items.text: Some sea cucumbers shoot out their guts to tangle attackers.
items.reason: This is how they defend themselves, not how they help the reef.

encounters.frame: Tully is reading the island newspaper aloud by torchlight. The Gistling's feathers are on end.
encounters.text: For three nights in a row, fishers off Hollowgum Point reported a ship with no lights drifting silently past the headland. Some swore they saw a pale figure standing at the wheel. Others heard a low moaning sound carried across the water. By Wednesday, the island's chat groups were full of talk about a ghost ship, and one local café started selling 'Phantom Pies'. On Thursday morning, the coast guard finally went out to take a look. What they found was a lot less frightening than a ghost. The 'ghost ship' was an old cargo boat that had broken free from its mooring on the mainland during a storm and floated more than eighty kilometres. Nobody was on board. Its hold contained nothing but a pile of old fishing nets. The pale figure at the wheel turned out to be a white raincoat hung on a hook, flapping in the wind. The moaning came from a loose metal door, swinging and scraping on its hinges every time the boat rolled. The coast guard towed the boat back to port, where its owner said he was relieved, and slightly embarrassed. The café is still selling Phantom Pies, though, and says business has never been better.
encounters.prompt: Which headline fits the report best?
encounters.success: The report builds a spooky mystery, then explains it all. The runaway boat is the big idea.

Ghost ship haunts Hollowgum Point
options.reason: That's what people feared at first. The report shows the ship wasn't haunted at all.

options.reason: The pies are a funny side story, not what the report is mostly about.

options.text: Mystery raincoat spotted flapping at the wheel of drifting boat
options.reason: The raincoat explains one spooky sighting. A headline should cover the whole report.

encounters.frame: Zed is reading an astronaut's blog to the crew at dinner.
encounters.prompt: Tap the sentence that tells the main idea.
encounters.success: Teeth, hair, tears, hands and socks are all tiny jobs made hard by space. That sentence sums them up.

parts.tap: The launch was loud and shaky, but it was over in under ten minutes.
parts.reason: This tells you the launch wasn't the hard part. It sets up the main idea.

parts.tap: What I wasn't ready for was how difficult the tiniest everyday jobs would become.

Washing my hands involves a damp cloth and a lot of patience. Cutting my hair means using clippers attached to a vacuum hose, otherwise the clippings drift into the air filters.

parts.tap: Even crying is tricky: without gravity, tears don't roll down your cheeks but collect in a wobbly ball over your eye.
parts.reason: A surprising fact about one thing, not what the blog is mostly about.

parts: Getting dressed is a battle, because your socks try to swim away the moment you let go of them.
